title: Retrograde Program Analysis: A Practical Tutorial
abstract: Retrograde analysis reads programs from the end to the beginning: treat statements as constraints on prior states, propagate sets of states backward, and compare the reachable inputs with the intended specification. This tutorial condenses a longer exposition to a focused guide with definitions, worked examples (toy branches, sorting networks, binary search), loop treatment via fixpoints, and a range-algebra appendix that standardizes array splits and midpoints. The aim is practical: short proofs, concrete invariants, and drop-in code and property tests
gemini_output:
\noindent\textbf{1. BACKGROUND \& CONTEXT}\\
This research provides a practical guide to "Retrograde Program Analysis," a method for understanding software by reading its execution in reverse, from the end state back to the initial inputs. The study is important because it offers a systematic way to verify if a program's outcomes match its intended specifications by treating each statement as a constraint on prior states. Key concepts include backward state propagation, fixpoints for loop analysis, and a specialized range algebra for handling data structures like arrays. This approach provides a rigorous framework for software verification, simplifying complex proofs and offering concrete insights into program behavior.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{2. REAL-WORLD PROBLEMS SOLVED}\\
The paper directly addresses the challenge of ensuring program correctness and reliability, a critical need in all software development. It solves the problem of verifying whether a program can achieve a specific output or if its inputs align with an intended specification by effectively tracing backwards. At TRL 2-3 (concept formulated and analytically validated), this method provides a powerful diagnostic tool for developers to identify unexpected program behaviors or prove the absence of certain flaws. Advancing this work would require integrating these techniques into automated verification tools for real-world software projects.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{3. MARKET ANALYSIS}\\
The market for software quality assurance, static analysis, and formal verification tools is robust and growing, driven by the increasing complexity and criticality of software systems. There is strong industry demand for methods that reduce bugs, improve security, and meet compliance standards, particularly in sectors like automotive, aerospace, and finance. While competitors include existing static analyzers and testing frameworks, retrograde analysis offers a unique backward-looking perspective that complements these tools. Adoption challenges include the need for specialized expertise in formal methods, but the tutorial's practical aim helps lower this barrier, making collaboration with software tool vendors an attractive path.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{4. IMMEDIATE IDEAS FOR STARTUPS/PATENTS}\\
While the tutorial itself is unpatentable, specific novel algorithms or highly efficient implementations of retrograde analysis for particular programming languages or domains could be. A viable startup could develop specialized software tools that automate retrograde analysis, integrating it into existing development environments (IDEs) or CI/CD pipelines to enhance code verification. Companies focused on static analysis, cybersecurity, or formal verification might license advanced components of this methodology to improve their product offerings. A practical next step involves creating open-source libraries or commercial plugins that implement the described techniques, providing developers with readily accessible verification capabilities.

title: Range Algebra for Safe Array Splits
abstract: We present a language-agnostic range algebra that derives correct index intervals for splitting arrays and implementing binary search, eliminating off-by-one and empty-range bugs. From two primitives -- $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ and $\lceil n/2\rceil = \lfloor (n + 1)/2\rfloor$ -- we obtain four canonical splits (Natural, Left+, Right+, Center-cut) with proofs of coverage and balance for all $n \ge 0$ and any base index $b \in \mathbb{Z}$. We record invariants (normalization to left-closed/right-open intervals $[u, w)$ with len $= w - u$), document cross-language division quirks, and give drop-in code patterns and property tests. The result is a small, memorable spec that can be copied verbatim into C/C++/Java/C\#/Go/Rust/Swift/JS/Python.

This research introduces a novel "range algebra" designed to precisely define index intervals for splitting arrays and implementing algorithms like binary search, eliminating common programming errors. It is crucial because off-by-one and empty-range bugs are pervasive and costly in software development. The study builds on two fundamental division primitives, $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ and $\lceil n/2\rceil$, to derive four canonical splitting patterns, providing formal proofs for their correctness across all array sizes and base indices. This work aims to establish a universally correct and memorable specification for handling array subdivisions.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{2. REAL-WORLD PROBLEMS SOLVED}\\
The paper directly addresses the chronic problem of subtle yet critical indexing errors, such as off-by-one mistakes and the creation of invalid empty ranges, that frequently occur in array manipulation and search algorithms. These bugs lead to unexpected program behavior, crashes, and significant debugging time for developers across various programming languages. By providing a small, formally proven set of rules and code patterns, this research helps developers write more robust, reliable, and secure software. At TRL 2 (concept formulated), this theoretical framework offers a practical guide to eliminate a widespread class of software defects.

title: Texture-Aware Superpixel Segmentation
abstract: Most superpixel algorithms compute a trade-off between spatial and color features at the pixel level. Hence, they may need fine parameter tuning to balance the two measures, and highly fail to group pixels with similar local texture properties. In this paper, we address these issues with a new Texture-Aware SuperPixel (TASP) method. To accurately segment textured and smooth areas, TASP automatically adjusts its spatial constraint according to the local feature variance. Then, to ensure texture homogeneity within superpixels, a new pixel to superpixel patch-based distance is proposed. TASP outperforms the segmentation accuracy of the state-of-the-art methods on texture and also natural color image datasets.

TASP addresses this by automatically adjusting its behavior based on local image characteristics, making it more robust and accurate for both textured and smooth areas. title: Superpixel-based Color Transfer
abstract: In this work, we propose a fast superpixel-based color transfer method (SCT) between two images. Superpixels enable to decrease the image dimension and to extract a reduced set of color candidates. We propose to use a fast approximate nearest neighbor matching algorithm in which we enforce the match diversity by limiting the selection of the same superpixels. A fusion framework is designed to transfer the matched colors, and we demonstrate the improvement obtained over exact matching results. Finally, we show that SCT is visually competitive compared to state-of-the-art methods.

title: SCALP: Superpixels with Contour Adherence using Linear Path
abstract: Superpixel decomposition methods are generally used as a pre-processing step to speed up image processing tasks. They group the pixels of an image into homogeneous regions while trying to respect existing contours. For all state-of-the-art superpixel decomposition methods, a trade-off is made between 1) computational time, 2) adherence to image contours and 3) regularity and compactness of the decomposition. In this paper, we propose a fast method to compute Superpixels with Contour Adherence using Linear Path (SCALP) in an iterative clustering framework. The distance computed when trying to associate a pixel to a superpixel during the clustering is enhanced by considering the linear path to the superpixel barycenter. The proposed framework produces regular and compact superpixels that adhere to the image contours. We provide a detailed evaluation of SCALP on the standard Berkeley Segmentation Dataset. The obtained results outperform state-of-the-art methods in terms of standard superpixel and contour detection metrics.

The study is important because existing superpixel methods consistently face a fundamental trade-off between computational speed, how well they align with actual object boundaries (contour adherence), and the regularity and compactness of the generated regions. SCALP aims to resolve this compromise, offering a superior balance of these crucial performance aspects.

This innovation allows SCALP to generate regular, compact superpixels that meticulously adhere to image contours, outperforming state-of-the-art methods. title: Blind Network Revenue Management and Bandits with Knapsacks under Limited Switches
abstract: This paper studies the impact of limited switches on resource-constrained dynamic pricing with demand learning. We focus on the classical price-based blind network revenue management problem and extend our results to the bandits with knapsacks problem. In both settings, a decision maker faces stochastic and distributionally unknown demand, and must allocate finite initial inventory across multiple resources over time. In addition to standard resource constraints, we impose a switching constraint that limits the number of action changes over the time horizon. We establish matching upper and lower bounds on the optimal regret and develop computationally efficient limited-switch algorithms that achieve it. We show that the optimal regret rate is fully characterized by a piecewise-constant function of the switching budget, which further depends on the number of resource constraints. Our results highlight the fundamental role of resource constraints in shaping the statistical complexity of online learning under limited switches. Extensive simulations demonstrate that our algorithms maintain strong cumulative reward performance while significantly reducing the number of switches.

title: Dynamic traversal of large gaps by insects and legged robots reveals a template
abstract: It is well known that animals can use neural and sensory feedback via vision, tactile sensing, and echolocation to negotiate obstacles. Similarly, most robots use deliberate or reactive planning to avoid obstacles, which relies on prior knowledge or high-fidelity sensing of the environment. However, during dynamic locomotion in complex, novel, 3-D terrains such as forest floor and building rubble, sensing and planning suffer bandwidth limitation and large noise and are sometimes even impossible. Here, we study rapid locomotion over a large gap, a simple, ubiquitous obstacle, to begin to discover general principles of dynamic traversal of large 3-D obstacles. We challenged the discoid cockroach and an open-loop six-legged robot to traverse a large gap of varying length. Both the animal and the robot could dynamically traverse a gap as large as 1 body length by bridging the gap with its head, but traversal probability decreased with gap length. Based on these observations, we developed a template that well captured body dynamics and quantitatively predicted traversal performance. Our template revealed that high approach speed, initial body pitch, and initial body pitch angular velocity facilitated dynamic traversal, and successfully predicted a new strategy of using body pitch control that increased the robot maximal traversal gap length by 50%. Our study established the first template of dynamic locomotion beyond planar surfaces and is an important step in expanding terradynamics into complex 3-D terrains.

By focusing on rapid locomotion over simple, ubiquitous gaps, this work aims to uncover general principles for robust movement in challenging 3D terrains, expanding the foundational field of terradynamics beyond flat surfaces.

This research, at TRL 2-3 (concept formulated and experimentally validated), develops a quantitative "template" that accurately predicts this dynamic behavior. Critically, applying this template has already led to a new strategy that increased the robot's maximal traversal gap length by 50% using simple body pitch control.

title: Body-terrain interaction affects large bump traversal of insects and legged robots
abstract: Small animals and robots must often rapidly traverse large bump-like obstacles when moving through complex 3-D terrains, during which, in addition to leg-ground contact, their body inevitably comes into physical contact with the obstacles. However, we know little about the performance limits of large bump traversal and how body-terrain interaction affects traversal. To address these, we challenged the discoid cockroach and an open-loop six-legged robot to dynamically run into a large bump of varying height to discover the maximal traversal performance, and studied how locomotor modes and traversal performance are affected by body-terrain interaction. Remarkably, during rapid running, both the animal and the robot were capable of dynamically traversing a bump much higher than its hip height (up to 4 times the hip height for the animal and 3 times for the robot, respectively) at traversal speeds typical of running, with decreasing traversal probability with increasing bump height. A stability analysis using a novel locomotion energy landscape model explained why traversal was more likely when the animal or robot approached the bump with a low initial body yaw and a high initial body pitch, and why deflection was more likely otherwise. Inspired by these principles, we demonstrated a novel control strategy of active body pitching that increased the robot maximal traversable bump height by 75%. Our study is a major step in establishing the framework of locomotion energy landscapes to understand locomotion in complex 3-D terrains.

title: Robotic modeling of snake traversing large, smooth obstacles reveals stability benefits of body compliance
abstract: Snakes can move through almost any terrain. Although their locomotion on flat surfaces using planar gaits is inherently stable, when snakes deform their body out of plane to traverse complex terrain, maintaining stability becomes a challenge. On trees and desert dunes, snakes grip branches or brace against depressed sand for stability. However, how they stably surmount obstacles like boulders too large and smooth to gain such anchor points is less understood. Similarly, snake robots are challenged to stably traverse large, smooth obstacles for search and rescue and building inspection. Our recent study discovered that snakes combine body lateral undulation and cantilevering to stably traverse large steps. Here, we developed a snake robot with this gait and snake-like anisotropic friction and used it as a physical model to understand stability principles. The robot traversed steps as high as a third of its body length rapidly and stably. However, on higher steps, it was more likely to fail due to more frequent rolling and flipping over, which was absent in the snake with a compliant body. Adding body compliance reduced the robot roll instability by statistically improving surface contact, without reducing speed. Besides advancing understanding of snake locomotion, our robot achieved high traversal speed surpassing most previous snake robots and approaching snakes, while maintaining high traversal probability.
gemini_output:

The study utilizes a snake robot, designed with specific snake-like gaits and friction properties, as a physical model to uncover the underlying mechanical principles that allow for stable movement when the body must deform out of a flat plane.

title: Joint data imputation and mechanistic modelling for simulating heart-brain interactions in incomplete datasets
abstract: The use of mechanistic models in clinical studies is limited by the lack of multi-modal patients data representing different anatomical and physiological processes. For example, neuroimaging datasets do not provide a sufficient representation of heart features for the modeling of cardiovascular factors in brain disorders. To tackle this problem we introduce a probabilistic framework for joint cardiac data imputation and personalisation of cardiovascular mechanistic models, with application to brain studies with incomplete heart data. Our approach is based on a variational framework for the joint inference of an imputation model of cardiac information from the available features, along with a Gaussian Process emulator that can faithfully reproduce personalised cardiovascular dynamics. Experimental results on UK Biobank show that our model allows accurate imputation of missing cardiac features in datasets containing minimal heart information, e.g. systolic and diastolic blood pressures only, while jointly estimating the emulated parameters of the lumped model. This allows a novel exploration of the heart-brain joint relationship through simulation of realistic cardiac dynamics corresponding to different conditions of brain anatomy.
gemini_output:

This innovative approach helps overcome data limitations that currently hinder comprehensive physiological modeling.

\noindent\textbf{4. IMMEDIATE IDEAS FOR STARTUPS/PATENTS}\\
This probabilistic framework presents a strong case for patenting, particularly for its novel combination of data imputation and mechanistic model personalization. A viable startup could emerge by developing a software platform that offers this joint imputation and simulation capability as a service to clinical researchers and pharmaceutical companies. Another path involves licensing the framework to existing health analytics or AI-driven diagnostic firms to enhance their predictive modeling with incomplete patient data, allowing them to offer more comprehensive insights into conditions like stroke or dementia.

title: The infinite information gap between mathematical and physical representations
abstract: Partial orders have been used to model several experimental setups, going from classical thermodynamics and general relativity to the quantum realm with its resource theories. In order to study such experimental setups, one typically characterizes them via a (numerical) representation, that is, a set of real-valued functions. In the context of resource theory, it is customary to use \textbf{mathematical} representations, i.e. a set of \textbf{measurement outcomes} which characterize the achievable transitions within the experimental setup. However, in line with the minimum energy and maximum entropy principles in classical mechanics and thermodynamics, respectively, one would expect an optimization interpretation for a representation to be called \textbf{physical}. More specifically, a physical representation could consist of a set of competing \textbf{optimization principles} such that a transition happens provided they are all optimized by it. Somewhat surprisingly, we show that this distinction can result in an \textbf{infinite information gap}, with some partial orders having mathematical representations that involve a finite amount of information and requiring infinite information to build a physical representation. We connect this phenomenon with well-known resource-theoretic scenarios like majorization, and develop notions of partial order dimension that run in parallel to the representations that we consider. Our results improve on the classification of preordered spaces in terms of real-valued functions.
gemini_output:
\noindent\textbf{1. BACKGROUND \& CONTEXT}\\
This research critically examines how experimental systems, from classical thermodynamics to quantum resource theories, are mathematically modeled using "partial orders." It explores two distinct ways these systems are characterized: "mathematical representations," which rely on simple measurement outcomes, and "physical representations," which are based on optimizing principles like minimum energy. Understanding this distinction is vital because it reveals fundamental differences in how we describe and predict system behavior, highlighting whether our models truly capture the underlying physical reality or merely a mathematical convenience.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{2. REAL-WORLD PROBLEMS SOLVED}\\
The paper addresses a significant conceptual problem: the potential for an "infinite information gap" between our mathematical descriptions of physical systems and their actual physical behavior. It proves that certain systems, despite having straightforward mathematical models, might demand an infinite amount of information to be accurately described by physically meaningful optimization principles. This finding challenges the completeness of current theoretical frameworks, particularly in quantum resource theories, by demonstrating that simply observing "what happens" (mathematical) may not adequately explain "why it happens" (physical), leading to potential misinterpretations of system capabilities and limitations.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{3. MARKET ANALYSIS}\\
This foundational research holds indirect but significant market relevance for fields like quantum information, AI, and complex systems modeling, where resource theories are applied. While not an immediate product, its insights could improve the theoretical underpinnings for designing more robust quantum algorithms, AI optimization strategies, or even drug discovery simulations by clarifying the boundaries of what models can accurately represent. Adoption challenges stem from its highly theoretical nature, requiring further translational research, but it offers critical validation criteria for academic and R\&D efforts focused on developing truly "physical" representations for new technologies.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{4. IMMEDIATE IDEAS FOR STARTUPS/PATENTS}\\
This theoretical work, by exposing a fundamental limit rather than offering a direct invention, is unpatentable and unlikely to lead to a standalone startup. However, it provides invaluable guidance for developers of advanced simulation and modeling software, particularly for quantum systems or resource-constrained AI. Companies building quantum compilers or optimization platforms could integrate these findings to identify instances where a mathematical model might oversimplify the underlying physical constraints, ensuring that proposed "speedups" or "optimizations" are physically achievable. This research serves as a theoretical benchmark, driving the development of more accurate and physically consistent computational tools.

title: The Surface Edge Explorer (SEE): A measurement-direct approach to next best view planning
abstract:
High-quality observations of the real world are crucial for a variety of applications, including producing 3D printed replicas of small-scale scenes and conducting inspections of large-scale infrastructure. These 3D observations are commonly obtained by combining multiple sensor measurements from different views. Guiding the selection of suitable views is known as the NBV planning problem.
  Most NBV approaches reason about measurements using rigid data structures (e.g., surface meshes or voxel grids). This simplifies next best view selection but can be computationally expensive, reduces real-world fidelity, and couples the selection of a next best view with the final data processing.
  This paper presents the Surface Edge Explorer, a NBV approach that selects new observations directly from previous sensor measurements without requiring rigid data structures. SEE uses measurement density to propose next best views that increase coverage of insufficiently observed surfaces while avoiding potential occlusions. Statistical results from simulated experiments show that SEE can attain similar or better surface coverage with less observation time and travel distance than evaluated volumetric approaches on both small- and large-scale scenes. Real-world experiments demonstrate SEE autonomously observing a deer statue using a 3D sensor affixed to a robotic arm.
gemini_output:
\noindent\textbf{1. BACKGROUND \& CONTEXT}\\
This research introduces the Surface Edge Explorer (SEE), an innovative method for Next Best View (NBV) planning, which is essential for creating high-quality 3D models from multiple sensor measurements. The study addresses the inefficiencies of current NBV techniques, which rely on rigid data structures that increase computational cost and reduce real-world accuracy. SEE directly analyzes previous sensor data to propose optimal new views, aiming to improve surface coverage and avoid occlusions. This approach is vital for advancing automated 3D reconstruction in diverse applications.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{2. REAL-WORLD PROBLEMS SOLVED}\\
The paper solves the critical problem of inefficient and often inaccurate 3D scanning, where current "Next Best View" (NBV) planning systems are hampered by rigid data structures. These conventional methods are computationally expensive, reduce the fidelity of the final 3D model, and slow down the observation process. The Surface Edge Explorer (SEE) overcomes this by directly analyzing sensor measurements to propose new views, significantly improving surface coverage while reducing observation time and travel distance. This innovation streamlines the process of acquiring comprehensive 3D data for complex objects and environments.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{3. MARKET ANALYSIS}\\
The market for high-quality 3D observations is substantial, driven by demand in sectors like manufacturing, infrastructure inspection, and digital replication. Current 3D scanning solutions, while functional, often struggle with efficiency and accuracy due to their reliance on rigid data structures. This research presents a strong competitive advantage by offering a more direct and less computationally intensive approach to Next Best View planning. Startups and established companies in robotics, automated inspection, and 3D printing could integrate this technology to enhance their offerings and reduce operational costs, making it particularly appealing for applications requiring rapid and precise 3D data acquisition.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{4. IMMEDIATE IDEAS FOR STARTUPS/PATENTS}\\
This research offers strong potential for intellectual property protection through method patents covering the novel measurement-direct approach to Next Best View planning. A viable startup could develop and license software integrating the Surface Edge Explorer (SEE) algorithm, providing advanced automated 3D scanning capabilities for industrial inspection, quality control, or digital twin creation. This could also be integrated as a specialized module into existing robotic operating systems or hardware platforms. Next steps could involve developing a commercial software package or an SDK that allows manufacturers and service providers to adopt SEE for more efficient and accurate 3D data acquisition.

title: Low-Stabilizer-Complexity Quantum States Are Not Pseudorandom
abstract:
We show that quantum states with "low stabilizer complexity" can be efficiently distinguished from Haar-random. Specifically, given an $n$-qubit pure state $|ψ\rangle$, we give an efficient algorithm that distinguishes whether $|ψ\rangle$ is (i) Haar-random or (ii) a state with stabilizer fidelity at least $\frac{1}{k}$ (i.e., has fidelity at least $\frac{1}{k}$ with some stabilizer state), promised that one of these is the case. With black-box access to $|ψ\rangle$, our algorithm uses $O\!\left( k^{12} \log(1/δ)\right)$ copies of $|ψ\rangle$ and $O\!\left(n k^{12} \log(1/δ)\right)$ time to succeed with probability at least $1-δ$, and, with access to a state preparation unitary for $|ψ\rangle$ (and its inverse), $O\!\left( k^{3} \log(1/δ)\right)$ queries and $O\!\left(n k^{3} \log(1/δ)\right)$ time suffice.
  As a corollary, we prove that $ω(\log(n))$ $T$-gates are necessary for any Clifford+$T$ circuit to prepare computationally pseudorandom quantum states, a first-of-its-kind lower bound.
gemini_output:
\noindent\textbf{1. BACKGROUND \& CONTEXT}\\
This research fundamentally examines the security properties of quantum states, specifically investigating whether "simple" quantum states, characterized by low stabilizer complexity, can be effectively distinguished from truly random, or Haar-random, states. The study is critical for understanding the limits of quantum pseudorandomness, which underpins the security of many quantum cryptographic protocols. Key concepts include stabilizer states (a class of easily prepared quantum states) and their fidelity, and the efficiency of distinguishing these from arbitrary random states. Historically, it was often assumed that even relatively simple quantum circuits could generate states indistinguishable from random, but this work provides a rigorous method to demonstrate otherwise.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{2. REAL-WORLD PROBLEMS SOLVED}\\
The paper addresses a critical challenge in quantum cryptography and computation: ensuring the pseudorandomness of quantum states used in secure applications. It proves that quantum states generated with low "stabilizer complexity" or a limited number of T-gates (a specific type of quantum operation) are not truly pseudorandom, meaning they can be efficiently identified and thus are unsuitable for tasks requiring genuine randomness. At TRL 2 (concept formulated), this theoretical insight clarifies that using computationally "cheap" quantum states might compromise security, providing a crucial lower bound on the resources needed for secure quantum operations. Advancing requires integrating these bounds into practical quantum security assessments.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{3. MARKET ANALYSIS}\\
The quantum security market, though nascent, is rapidly growing due to the threat of quantum computers breaking classical encryption. Demand exists for robust methods to generate and verify truly random or pseudorandom quantum states for cryptographic keys and secure communication. This research offers foundational insights for quantum hardware and software developers, particularly those designing quantum random number generators or cryptographic primitives. Competitors include other approaches to quantum randomness generation, but this work uniquely establishes a fundamental limit on how simple a state can be while still appearing random. Regulatory hurdles are minimal, but industry collaboration is crucial for translating theoretical bounds into practical security standards.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{4. IMMEDIATE IDEAS FOR STARTUPS/PATENTS}\\
The core finding of this research—a mathematical lower bound and a distinguishing algorithm—is likely unpatentable. However, it provides valuable intellectual property for informing quantum software development. Startups could develop auditing tools or software libraries that verify the pseudorandomness of quantum states generated by specific circuits, especially for cryptographic applications. For instance, quantum compiler developers could integrate these findings to automatically flag circuits that don't meet minimum T-gate requirements for pseudorandomness. A viable startup could emerge by focusing on certification or benchmarking services for quantum hardware's randomness capabilities, leveraging this understanding to ensure security compliance.

title: Quantum Cryptography in Algorithmica
abstract:
We construct a classical oracle relative to which $\mathsf{P} = \mathsf{NP}$ yet single-copy secure pseudorandom quantum states exist. In the language of Impagliazzo's five worlds, this is a construction of pseudorandom states in "Algorithmica," and hence shows that in a black-box setting, quantum cryptography based on pseudorandom states is possible even if one-way functions do not exist. As a consequence, we demonstrate that there exists a property of a cryptographic hash function that simultaneously (1) suffices to construct pseudorandom states, (2) holds for a random oracle, and (3) is independent of $\mathsf{P}$ vs. $\mathsf{NP}$ in the black-box setting. We also introduce a conjecture that would generalize our results to multi-copy secure pseudorandom states.
  We build on the recent construction by Aaronson, Ingram, and Kretschmer (CCC 2022) of an oracle relative to which $\mathsf{P} = \mathsf{NP}$ but $\mathsf{BQP} \neq \mathsf{QCMA}$, based on hardness of the OR $\circ$ Forrelation problem. Our proof also introduces a new discretely-defined variant of the Forrelation distribution, for which we prove pseudorandomness against $\mathsf{AC^0}$ circuits. This variant may be of independent interest.
gemini_output:
\noindent\textbf{1. BACKGROUND \& CONTEXT}\\
This research fundamentally re-examines the assumptions behind quantum cryptography by exploring the conditions under which secure quantum states can exist. Specifically, it investigates "pseudorandom quantum states" (PRQS), which are quantum counterparts to classical pseudorandom numbers, designed to be indistinguishable from truly random states. The study is critical because it demonstrates that, in a theoretical "black-box" setting, PRQS can be constructed even if fundamental classical cryptographic assumptions, like the existence of one-way functions (where P=NP), do not hold. This finding challenges the conventional wisdom that all cryptography relies on computational hardness, opening new avenues for understanding quantum security.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{2. REAL-WORLD PROBLEMS SOLVED}\\
The paper addresses a foundational conceptual problem: whether quantum cryptography can exist independently of the computational hardness assumptions (like one-way functions) that underpin classical cryptography. It proves that single-copy secure pseudorandom quantum states are possible even in a scenario ("Algorithmica") where P=NP, meaning problems that are quickly verifiable are also quickly solvable. This theoretical insight at TRL 1 (basic principles observed) clarifies that certain quantum cryptographic primitives possess unique security properties not tied to classical complexity, suggesting a different basis for quantum security. Advancing requires exploring multi-copy security and the implications for practical quantum key distribution or secure computation.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{3. MARKET ANALYSIS}\\
The market for quantum cryptography is nascent, driven by long-term strategic needs for quantum-resistant security rather than immediate product adoption. This theoretical work offers foundational insights rather than a deployable solution, making its direct market impact limited. However, it contributes to the academic and research ecosystem that informs future quantum security standards. Demand exists for robust cryptographic primitives, but current challenges include the immaturity of quantum hardware and the abstract nature of P=NP questions. Competitors include other quantum-safe cryptography methods, but this research distinguishes itself by exploring security without one-way functions. Regulatory frameworks are years away, but these insights could shape future quantum security protocols.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{4. IMMEDIATE IDEAS FOR STARTUPS/PATENTS}\\
This research is a theoretical proof of existence rather than an invention, making it unpatentable in its current form. It primarily contributes to fundamental knowledge in quantum information theory. A direct startup based on this work is not feasible, as it doesn't offer a product. However, the findings are invaluable for informing the design of future quantum cryptographic protocols. For instance, developers of quantum security frameworks or quantum algorithm designers could leverage these insights to build systems that exploit cryptographic properties independent of classical one-way functions, potentially leading to novel quantum-resistant solutions. A practical next step involves further theoretical work to extend these findings to multi-copy secure states and explore concrete protocol designs based on these unique quantum properties.

title: Quantum Mass Production Theorems
abstract: We prove that for any $n$-qubit unitary transformation $U$ and for any $r = 2^{o(n / \log n)}$, there exists a quantum circuit to implement $U^{\otimes r}$ with at most $O(4^n)$ gates. This asymptotically equals the number of gates needed to implement just a single copy of a worst-case $U$. We also establish analogous results for quantum states and diagonal unitary transformations. Our techniques are based on the work of Uhlig [Math. Notes 1974], who proved a similar mass production theorem for Boolean functions.
gemini_output:
\noindent\textbf{1. BACKGROUND \& CONTEXT}\\
This research fundamentally re-examines the efficiency of creating multiple copies of quantum operations and states, a process often assumed to be linearly costly. The study reveals that for a sufficiently large number of copies ($r = 2^{o(n / \log n)}$), an $n$-qubit unitary operation \(U\) can be implemented \(r\) times ($U^{\otimes r}$) with a total gate count ($O(4^n)$) that is only asymptotically equal to creating just a single copy of a worst-case \(U\). This is significant because it challenges the conventional understanding of resource scaling in quantum computation, drawing parallels to similar "mass production" theorems found in classical Boolean functions.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{2. REAL-WORLD PROBLEMS SOLVED}\\
The paper addresses the critical problem of resource efficiency in scaling quantum algorithms, where duplicating complex quantum operations or states can quickly become a computational bottleneck. By proving that many copies can be generated with a cost approaching that of a single copy, this work offers a theoretical pathway to overcome this challenge. It provides a foundational understanding that could enable the "mass production" of quantum components, making large-scale quantum simulations or computations, which often require repeated applications of the same unitary, far more feasible. At TRL 2 (concept formulated), this theoretical breakthrough requires validation through its integration into quantum circuit design tools.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{3. MARKET ANALYSIS}\\
The emerging quantum computing market urgently seeks methods to reduce the resource cost and complexity of quantum circuits. This research directly supports the demand for more efficient quantum software and algorithms by demonstrating a path to drastically optimize repeated operations. While the market is nascent, any development that improves scalability or reduces gate counts holds significant value for quantum software developers, hardware manufacturers, and end-users running complex quantum simulations. The challenge lies in translating these theoretical theorems into practical compiler optimizations, offering a competitive advantage over existing, less efficient circuit synthesis methods.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{4. IMMEDIATE IDEAS FOR STARTUPS/PATENTS}\\
While the core mathematical theorems themselves are likely not patentable, their application in novel quantum circuit compilation techniques or specific algorithm implementations could be. A startup could focus on developing advanced quantum compilers that automatically identify and apply these "mass production" optimizations to quantum circuits, particularly for algorithms in quantum machine learning or chemistry simulations that involve repeated unitary operations. Such a company could license its optimized compiler technology to quantum hardware providers or cloud-based quantum computing platforms. A practical next step involves integrating these theoretical insights into open-source quantum programming frameworks to demonstrate their real-world impact on circuit depth and gate counts.
